book: 038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive

chapters.relation: Sean Burt argues that despite its Orwellian dystopian surface — the internalized mind control of "2 + 2 = 5" ("I'll stay home forever, where two and two always makes five"), the commands of "Sit Down. Stand Up.," the hunted domesticity of "A Wolf at the Door" — Hail to the Thief is genuinely utopian thought in Ernst Bloch's and Fredric Jameson's sense: imagining any different world, even a repressive one, breaks capitalism's "eternal present" and keeps the future open. He traces fleeting glimmers of hope in "Sail to the Moon" and in "I Will"'s move from bunker to "I will rise up," each quickly shut down again by "Backdrifts" and "Where I End and You Begin" yet never fully renounced. The band's denials that the album is political matter because the album rejects both effective protest music (Against Me!'s ironic meta-protest) and ironic critical distance: we are not in on the joke, the joke is on us.

Brandon Forbes uses Hannah Arendt's distinction between power (people acting in concert, rooted in plurality and natality) and violence (instruments that ape power, one against all) to read Radiohead's violent imagery. The "Just" video shows that power lies not in what the prone man says but in everyone's collective act of lying down; "Sit Down. Stand Up." and "2 + 2 = 5" dramatize command backed by weapons and the revolutionary moment when a king's violence breeds the dissent that undoes him; "Life in a Glass House" and "Where I End and You Begin" depict totalitarian terror, the stage where violence has devoured power entirely. "I Will" ("I will rise up," "little babies' eyes") closes the chapter as Arendt's natality — the capacity of new political beginnings the gun can never defeat.

Jason Lee reads Hail to the Thief as a metaphysics of evil anchored in blurred boundaries between self and other: the "radiohead" conceit (Descartes' inert matter vs. thinking souls, Bowie's Thomas Newton) makes the sentient android of "Paranoid Android" the emblem of a self porous to signals and control, while "Where I End and You Begin" ("I will eat you alive") locates evil in the feared Other, glossed through Heidegger's das Nichts (evil as lack, not a thing) and Foucault's account of Enlightenment reason classing unreason as inhuman. He hears "Sit Down. Stand Up." as Auschwitz ("the raindrops could be gas") and "Go to Sleep" via The Wicker Man's human sacrifice, then argues The Most Gigantic Lying Mouth of All Time and Yorke's turn to Friends of the Earth and pay-what-you-want In Rainbows show philosophy is no longer sovereign: discourse with the Other is "responsibility, the call to respond ethically" — you have not been paying attention, so act before it's too late.

Adam Koehler reads Kid A's disfigured, barely intelligible vocals through Heidegger's account of how enabling technology withdraws into an invisible backdrop of everydayness: Pablo Honey hides its studio machinery behind "natural" rock, but Kid A — the cycled voice of "Everything in Its Right Place," the unintelligible vocoded "Kid A," "How to Disappear Completely" — forces the artifice itself into view, and with it the withdrawn world technology ordinarily conceals. The song is beautiful, he argues, because its willful failure to communicate feels human, enacting the anxiety of living in an information age that traps as much as it connects; John Mayer's lyric-clearing acoustic cover misses the point, since making sense now means risking not making sense, and the album's demand is that we listen to, and understand, everything withdrawn in the background.

chapters.file: ch27 - If You Think that You’re Strong Enough . ..md
chapters.relation: Matthew Lampert argues that Radiohead's stock theme of "alienation" is exactly Heideggerian inauthenticity: das Man's platitudes made audible in "Fitter Happier," the falling into the world's "uninhibited hustle" of "Ripcord" and "Let Down," and the tranquility that hides both the problem and any exit. He traces the band's arc from the punk-romantic fix of "Anyone Can Play Guitar" (choose and win yourself, form a band) to a deeper diagnosis on The Bends and OK Computer, where Heidegger's Ge-stell and standing-reserve show that in a technological framework only further technological solutions to technological alienation are available. Following "Why Poets?" and Holderlin's question, he concludes that Kid A makes Radiohead the poets in a desolate time: by risking disappearance itself ("How to Disappear Completely," "Idioteque") and singing alienation in its fullness rather than offering false hope, they stare into the abyss where "the more brightly do the ways into the saving power begin to shine."

Michael Thompson argues that the much-debated rhythm of "Pyramid Song" — 4/4 with syncopation, 3/3/4/3/3 groupings, or shifting signatures; Yorke says it is only "felt" — is philosophically pointed: by violating ordinary temporal expectations it forces an awareness of time itself, just as Chopin's nocturnes used time-signature changes to voice the nostalgia and melancholy of his Polish exile. Drawing on Gadamer's historically affected consciousness and the embodied, rhythmic daily life described by Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty, he reads the lyrics' row-boat to heaven ("all my past and futures") as a synoptic flash in which one sees past, present, and future as one organic whole. Because Yorke's heaven echoes Talking Heads' "Heaven" as a place where nothing happens, the song's consolation is that nothing lies outside our temporal embedding — with past and future united "there was nothing to fear and nothing to doubt."

chapters.file: ch29 - A Large Rock Saved My Life.md
chapters.relation: Lindsey Fiorelli reads OK Computer as Camus's absurd universe: "Subterranean Homesick Alien" and "Fitter Happier" portray a technological world drained of meaning, where to belong you must become a robotic "pig in a cage on antibiotics" and "Let Down" offers only the "emptiest of feelings." She stresses that Camus demands revolt, not escape — Sisyphus and Meursault embrace the absurd and thereby become happy — whereas Yorke's lyrics keep longing to flee (spaceships, growing wings, the resigned "No Surprises"). Yet the music itself embraces the technology the lyrics curse, and this, she concludes, is Radiohead's real Camusian move: like Camus writing novels about an alienating world, they carve Sisyphus's rock — modern technology, synthesizers and computers — into new and marvelous sounds, overcoming alienation by working within it.

chapters.file: ch31 - Today I Woke Up Sucking a Grammy.md
chapters.relation: Bradley Kaye reads Kid A as an album made under Lyotard's postmodern condition: "Everything in Its Right Place" ("what was that you tried to say?") and the murmured title track bear witness to the differend, something that must be put into phrases but cannot yet be; "The National Anthem" dramatizes incredulity toward the grand narrative of nationalism in favor of little narratives and local justice; "Treefingers" is the painful silence of the inexpressible, and "Optimistic" an ironic micro-political hope. The epigone problem (Yorke to Coldplay, Travis, and Muse: "Good luck with Kid A") and the closing Baudrillard turn — "In Limbo"'s "you're living in a fantasy world," the Marcus Welby and Perry Mason hyperreal, "it's not like the movies" — explain why even labeling the album "Best Alternative Album" Grammy presumes exactly the stable categories Kid A dissolves.

Tim Footman asks whether a rock band inside the media machine can avoid becoming a simulacrum of itself, tracing Radiohead's attempts to pierce Baudrillard's hyperreality: "Fake Plastic Trees" as the chain from plastic plants to plastic people, "Fitter Happier" as a simulacrum made of training-manual words, the no-singles Kid A campaign and leaked album, and the In Rainbows pay-what-you-want release that stripped away marketing — only to congeal into a new story about the band's anti-commercial perversity, since the free download was really advance publicity for a conventional for-sale album. Even seemingly authentic moments ("How I Made My Millions" recorded at home, the fabled Glastonbury 1997 set, Yorke's Dublin dissociation that became "How to Disappear Completely") are packaged slices of reality, so the band's melancholia is less a defeat of the simulacrum than a way of manifesting within it — "the best you can is good enough."

chapters.file: ch33 - How Come I End Up Where I Started.md
chapters.relation: Perry Owen Wright applies Baudrillard's Seduction to In Rainbows track by track: the Enlightenment reduced sex to anatomical biology and Natural Law, pornography is its hyperreal simulacrum (the HDTV of sex, played out in "Bodysnatchers"' "pale imitation with the edges sawn off"), and what re-enchants sex is seduction — an endless game of reversible signs, appearance and disappearance, aleatory suspension, and the trompe l'oeil's hypersimulation. "Weird Fishes/Arpeggi" shows the mortal risk of entering the game (the anglerfish's dangling false eyes), "All I Need" personifies Death itself as a stalker-seducer drawn into the loop of signs, "House of Cards" reads infidelity as leaving the game for the Law, and "Jigsaw Falling into Place" reduces seduction to production ending at the orgasm. "Videotape" closes the album at the pearly gates where even death becomes a sign to be seduced — the home movie "in red, blue, green" is the immortal sign we always leave behind.

chapters.file: ch35 - Where we got our big ideas.md

holes.name: Ernst Bloch
holes.what: German Marxist philosopher of hope whose The Principle of Hope distinguishes 'abstract utopia' (the diffuse impulse that things could be different, found in daydreams and art) from 'concrete utopia' (informed, planned commitment to change).
holes.why: Chapter 22's entire argument that Hail to the Thief's dystopia is utopian thought rests on Bloch's abstract/concrete utopia distinction.

holes.name: Fredric Jameson
holes.what: American Marxist literary critic who argues in Archaeologies of the Future that after the collapse of concrete utopias, utopian thought survives as the contemplation of an impossible break from capitalism's eternal present, for which dystopias are as essential as utopias.
holes.why: Chapter 22 leans on Jameson's framework to explain how the album's imagined totalitarian world functions as hope and critique of the here and now.

holes.name: Power vs Violence (natality)
holes.what: Arendt's distinction, in The Human Condition and On Violence, between power (people acting in concert, springing from plurality and the new beginnings of natality) and violence (instruments like weapons that counterfeit power and appear where power is in jeopardy).
holes.why: Chapter 23's whole reading of 'Just,' 'Sit Down. Stand Up.,' '2 + 2 = 5' and 'I Will' turns on this power/violence opposition and natality, which taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Alain Badiou
holes.what: French philosopher who ties philosophy to poetry as 'logical revolt' — thought pitted against the defective state of the world — and insists philosophy is part of the world rather than sovereign over it.
holes.why: Chapter 24 opens and closes with Badiou's philosophy-as-poetry-of-revolt as the frame for understanding Radiohead's project.

holes.name: Madness and Unreason (History of Madness)
holes.what: Foucault's account of how the classical age of reason constituted 'unreason' — madness — as the excluded, inhuman remainder of rationality, thereafter feared as the other of humanity.
holes.why: Chapter 24 uses this exclusion of unreason to explain how the feared Other of Hail to the Thief (evil, the inhuman, the 'terrorist') is produced by reason itself.

holes.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
holes.what: Heidegger's student whose Truth and Method develops 'historically effected consciousness': our awareness is determined by real past events, yet we can become conscious of this operativeness.
holes.why: Chapter 28's payoff for what 'Pyramid Song' makes audible is Gadamer's historically affected consciousness — life recognized as embedded in time.

holes.name: The Differend
holes.what: Lyotard's notion of the unstable state of language in which something that must be put into phrases cannot yet be, and literature or art bears witness to it by finding new idioms.
holes.why: Chapter 31 reads 'Everything in Its Right Place,' 'Kid A,' and 'Treefingers' specifically as bearing witness to the differend.

holes.name: Seduction (vs sex, desire, and production)
holes.what: Baudrillard's account (in Seduction) of seduction as an endless game of reversible signs, artifice, appearance and disappearance, Rules rather than Laws, that challenges the Enlightenment reduction of sex to biological desire and production.
holes.why: Chapter 33 applies seduction — aleatory suspension, the superficial abyss, trompe l'oeil, Rules vs Laws — to nearly every track on In Rainbows.
